source: Liu, Dubova, Conklin, Harada and Griffiths (2026, v3) Assessing the Effect of Cross-Domain Mapping on Creativity in Humans and LLMs
finding: Product-design task: a random source concept was given, or a user need. Humans gained originality from the random source. Seven LLMs gained nothing overall, but the benefit grew with source-target semantic distance, and only for the best LLMs.
numbers: 140 human idea-writers (Prolific), 7 LLMs, 1,002 raters (about 10 per idea). Cross-domain effect overall beta=0.36 (p<.001); human-by-source interaction beta=0.48. Distance predicts originality: humans beta=.1 (p<.01), LLMs beta=.18 (p<.001). o3 and Claude-Sonnet-4: all pairs beta=0.02 (p=.64); top 50% most distant pairs beta=0.12 (p=.029); top 10% beta=0.24 (p=.024). Pooled LLMs: initial deficit, n.s. once the closest 20% of pairs were dropped.
quote: the benefit of cross-domain mapping scales with semantic distance for both humans and LLMs
limits: One task family (product design from a target product plus a source). Distance from Wikipedia sentence embeddings and Jensen-Shannon divergence. Originality is rated by humans, not outcome-tested. Post-hoc subsetting of pairs, not a randomised distance manipulation.
agent_relevance: Closest direct test of O7/S3 seed distance on LLMs. Says: far seeds help only strong models and only when really remote; near or mid seeds do nothing or hurt. Use far seeds only for the strongest model and mark the distance threshold as a tunable.

source: Liu et al. (2026, v3) Cross-domain mapping: originality-feasibility trade-off
finding: Across ideas originality and feasibility trade off strongly. For humans the most original cross-domain ideas lose utility; equally original LLM ideas do not. Humans copy surface features of the source; LLMs copy structure and function.
numbers: Originality vs feasibility r=-0.74 (p<.001). Top 10% human cross-domain ideas vs LLM top 10%: originality equal (beta=0.02, p=.63) but less useful (beta=0.81, p<.001), less feasible (beta=0.26, p=.045), less worth investing (beta=0.60, p<.001). Example: a pickle desk, originality 4.78/5, utility 1.22/5. In the user-need condition the human top 10% matched LLMs on utility (beta=0.14, p=.20). Human and LLM originality for the same target-source pair correlate r=0.44 (p<.001).
limits: Top-10% comparison is by rating, with LLM and human pools of different size. Structure-transfer scores are hand-labelled on 1,400 cross-domain ideas.
agent_relevance: Distance buys novelty at a feasibility cost. The scaffold needs a fit check (critique state) after a far seed, and the LLM can transfer structure, which is the useful kind of transfer. Do not score seeds by distance alone.

source: Liu et al. (2026, v3) Methods and dose-response reading
finding: The dose-response analysis only drops close pairs step by step. The effect rises monotonically up to the top 10% most distant pairs. No upper limit of distance was tested, so no inverted-U can be seen or ruled out.
numbers: All pairs: n.s. for top LLMs; top 50%: beta=0.12; top 10%: beta=0.24. Humans were significant at every cut and larger as close pairs were removed.
limits: Subset analysis, with fewer pairs and wider CIs at the tail. Source concepts were everyday objects (octopus, toothbrush, pickle), so extreme irrelevance may be bounded.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 stays open: monotonic up to the tested range. Plan a dose-response run on our agent with a graded set of seed distances and a correctness check at the far end.

source: Chan, Siangliulue, McDonald, Liu, Moradinezhad, Aman, Solovey, Gajos and Dow (2017) Semantically Far Inspirations Considered Harmful? Accounting for Cognitive States in Collaborative Ideation
finding: Humans writing wedding-theme ideas. Always-far inspirations slowed ideation, cut within-category exploration and did not raise novelty; the best-novelty ideas of the far group were rated lower than the no-stimulus group. The associationist prediction (far is best) failed; the SIAM prediction (near while productive, far at impasse) fit better.
numbers: N=245 (MTurk), 1,574 ideas, 5 groups (no-stimuli 54, always-far 47, always-near 48, match-state 51, mismatch-state the rest). Max novelty: always-far 0.64 vs no-stimuli 0.88 (F(4,239)=2.5, p=.04; contrast t=-2.3, p=.07). Transition similarity 0.12 vs 0.19 (p<.01). Median inter-idea interval about 86 s vs 64 s (p=.02). Diversity: far above near (Tukey p=.01), not above control. Fluency equal: F(4,239)=0.5, p=.77.
quote: far inspirational ideas can harm creativity if received during productive ideation
limits: Humans, one theme, stimuli were other people's ideas (not seeds). Impasse detected by self-report request. Many contrasts, modest N. Table values read from a garbled text extraction; condition order inferred from the text.
agent_relevance: Strong boundary condition: distance helps when stuck, not while a line of exploration is productive. Gate far seeds on an impasse signal (open mode after cluster exhaustion), do not inject them by default.

source: Chan et al. (2017) fluency control and state effects
finding: Fluency was equal across conditions, so the weak or negative novelty result for far stimuli is not a fluency artefact in this design. Near stimuli during productive ideation made impasses rarer. Far stimuli did not help even though people used them.
numbers: 85% of participants in inspiration conditions used the feature. Fluency ANCOVA F(4,239)=0.5, p=.77. Baseline fluency vs novelty r=.03 (p=.68), vs transition similarity r=.02 (p=.79).
limits: No LLM. Fluency control is by design (idea counts), not the same as the Kenett 2014 first-10 control.
agent_relevance: Partly closes gap 2: a fixed number of ideas with far seeds does not by itself raise novelty. Seed variety is not the active ingredient; the match of seed to cognitive state may be.

source: Robinson, DeStefano, Vul and Brady (2024) Local but not global graph theoretic measures of semantic networks generalize across tasks
finding: Four experiments, each person doing two relatedness tasks on the same words. Local measures (how related is pot to pan) were reliable across tasks. Global network measures (average shortest path length, clustering) were not reliably stable within a person.
numbers: n=70 per experiment (1a, 1b, 2a, 2b), 20-word sets from Nelson norms. Average path length across tasks: weighted full graphs r=.11, .23, .14, -.014 (all n.s.); sparse weighted r=.204, .53 (p<.001, 1b only), -.032, -.076; binarised 33% density 1a partial r=.305 (p=.01, but not above the permuted null, p=1); 50% density 1b r=.478 (not above null). Clustering 1a weighted r=.053 (p=.663).
quote: metrics of global structural properties ... are less robust across tasks
limits: Small word sets (20 concepts) and student/online samples. Tests task-to-task reliability, not creativity validity. Fixed-edge and thresholded filtering change results.
agent_relevance: Path length per person is a weak individual signal. For the agent, use pairwise (local) seed-to-problem distance, not a global graph statistic. Weakens individual-level path-length claims.

source: Kenett, Beaty, Silvia, Anaki and Faust (2018) Flexibility of thought in high creative individuals represented by percolation analysis (PNAS)
finding: The semantic network of high-creative people is more robust when weak links are removed, so it stays connected longer. This is a re-analysis of the same data as the 2014 paper, not a new sample.
numbers: Percolation integral LSC 14.76 vs HSC 15.64. n=33 per group, selected from a pool of about 140 by a decision tree on RAT, TAU creativity test, divergent-thinking battery and a metaphor task. Result held under three Gaussian noise levels (Table 1).
quote: the semantic network of high creative individuals is more robust to network percolation
limits: Same 66 people as 2014; no independent sample; group-level network only; the percolation integral has no reported effect size.
agent_relevance: Closes the re-open item in gap 9 for the percolation numbers. Treat as same-sample support, not replication (gap 3 remains open).

source: Olson, Nahas, Chmoulevitch, Cropper and Webb (2021) Naming unrelated words predicts creativity (PNAS)
finding: The Divergent Association Task (name 10 unrelated words; mean embedding distance) correlates moderately with Alternative Uses scores. A second sample replicated the sign and size, and test-retest is good.
numbers: Study 1A N=141: manually screened r(55)=0.51 flexibility, 0.50 originality, 0.21 fluency (p=.057); full data r=0.34, 0.32, 0.22. Study 1B N=285 (no screening): r(223)=0.35, 0.32, 0.30. Bridge-the-Associative-Gap appropriateness r=0.22 to 0.23. Retest 2 weeks N=50 r(48)=0.73. Study 2: 8,572 participants from 98 countries (preregistered).
limits: Screening inflated Study 1A (.50 vs .32). Study 2 AUT link only in a small subset. Distance from one GloVe model.
agent_relevance: Closes the re-open item on Olson numbers. Distance is a modest, replicated predictor of originality (r about .3 unscreened). Expect small effects when seeding by distance.

source: Haase, Hanel and Pokutta (2025) S-DAT: A multilingual, GenAI-driven framework for automated divergent thinking assessment
finding: Replacing GloVe with eight multilingual LLM embedding models gave scores that correlate with the original DAT but with somewhat lower validity against AUT, and a narrower score distribution. The correlation with convergent thinking became non-significant.
numbers: S-DAT vs DAT agreement r=.65 in the large Olson Study 2 sample (n up to 8,498). DAT-AUT originality r=.32 in Study 1a (full data); S-DAT values reported as slightly lower on average. Eleven languages tested.
limits: Exact S-DAT AUT correlations could not be read cleanly from the extracted table. Calibrated by linear transform to the GloVe scale. Same datasets as Olson 2021.
agent_relevance: Metric choice shifts validity by a few hundredths to a tenth. Pick one embedding, calibrate it on a small human-rated set from our own task, and report which one.

source: Beaty and Johnson (2021) Automating creativity assessment with SemDis (Behavior Research Methods)
finding: Five semantic models (GloVe, CBOW and others) were combined into a latent semantic-distance factor, which predicted human creativity ratings across three AUT studies and novelty ratings in two word association studies.
numbers: Five studies. Coefficients not read this session (search snippet only).
limits: Snippet-level only. Exact r values to be read from the paper.
agent_relevance: Supports using an ensemble or latent factor of several embeddings, rather than one, as the seed-distance metric.

source: Organisciak, Acar, Dumas and Berthiaume (2023) Beyond semantic distance: automated scoring of divergent thinking greatly improves with large language models (Thinking Skills and Creativity)
finding: Fine-tuned LLM scorers (Ocsai) predict human originality ratings much better than raw semantic distance. A secondary summary also reports RoBERTa r=.72 and GPT-2 r=.70 vs semantic distance r=.42 on a metaphor task.
numbers: Up to r=.81 with human raters (project page, authors' own summary). Not verified in the paper text.
limits: Snippet and project page only; the .72/.70/.42 figures come from a different paper's search snippet.
agent_relevance: Distance is a cheap proxy; a trained or prompted judge is a better originality check than embedding distance. Use distance to choose seeds and a judge to score outputs.

source: Zhang, Yu, Chong, Sicilia, Tomz, Manning and Shi (2026, v4) Verbalized Sampling: How to mitigate mode collapse and unlock LLM diversity
finding: Asking one call for 5 responses with their probabilities (verbalized sampling) increases creative diversity over direct prompting, with human-rated diversity up and quality win-rates comparable. Bigger models gain more.
numbers: Semantic diversity 1.6 to 2.1 times direct prompting in poems, stories, jokes. Human study: 90 Prolific annotators (30 per task). Human diversity (1-4 scale) Direct vs Sequence vs VS-Standard: poem 1.90, 2.07, 2.39; story 2.74, 2.76, 3.06; joke 1.83, 2.93, 3.01. Larger models (GPT-4.1, Gemini-2.5-Pro) gain 1.5 to 2 times more diversity than small ones. Tunable by probability threshold in the prompt.
limits: Creative writing, dialogue, synthetic data; not problem-solving correctness. Quality by LLM rubric plus human win-rates. Sequence and VS-Standard lower quality for small models; VS-CoT and VS-Multi do not.
agent_relevance: A one-call diversity lever that needs no seed list. Candidate for open mode: ask for k options with probabilities, take the low-probability tail. Tokens roughly equal one k-candidate call.

source: Zhang et al. (2026) Verbalized Sampling: decoding ablations and downstream use
finding: Verbalized sampling combines with temperature, top-p and min-p. More candidates k means more diversity. It lifts diversity at every post-training stage (SFT, RLHF, RLVR) but cannot fully recover the base model. Diverse synthetic math data was used for downstream training.
numbers: Section F: diversity rises as the probability threshold is lowered; larger k gives more diversity. Table 3 downstream accuracy averaged over MATH500, OlympiadBench and Minerva (numbers not copied). Factual accuracy checked on SimpleQA (4,326 items).
limits: Downstream accuracy numbers and SimpleQA results were not read in detail this session.
agent_relevance: Supports that diversity can rise without hurting accuracy on checked tasks, but does not test far-seed injection or exclusion lists directly.

source: Ibrahim, Azad and Baten (2026) Anchorless Diversification for Parallel LLM Ideation
finding: Under full-pipeline token accounting, a population-referential 'stand out from other responses' instruction and a single planning call that splits the idea space into semantic directions give the best diversity-quality-per-token frontier. Anchoring on seed ideas (self, peer) can give larger raw diversity but costs 2 to 4 times the tokens.
numbers: GPT-5.4, Claude Sonnet 4.6, Gemini 2.5 Pro; pools of n=150 ideas; stories, AUT, slogans. The diverge instruction lifts pairwise diversity by 0.039 [0.030,0.049] (GPT-5.4) to 0.062 [0.053,0.072] (Claude) at token ratio 1.1. strat-diverge gain Claude 0.2526 vs best peer-anchor 0.2081; Gemini 0.1335 vs 0.1278; GPT-5.4 peer2 0.1719 vs strat 0.1730 with token ratio 3.71 vs 1.61. Diversity gain per 100k tokens (strat-diverge): GPT-5.4 0.295, Claude 0.379, Gemini 0.207. Quality-proxy gain per 100k tokens: 0.829, 1.211, 0.783.
limits: Quality is automatic proxies (e.g. MAoSS for stories), not task correctness. Peer anchoring has the best raw quality for two of three models. Preprint, May 2026.
agent_relevance: Direct answer to gap 6 on tokens: planning-call semantic directions and a population-referential instruction are cheap diversification; seed-anchor methods are not. No correctness task tested.

source: Nath, Dayan and Stevenson (2024) Characterising the Creative Process in Humans and Large Language Models
finding: Sentence embeddings group successive answers into categories, giving a jump profile from persistent (deep in few spaces) to flexible (many spaces). Humans: creativity not related to flexibility. LLMs: the more flexible models scored higher on originality. Temperature did not change the profile.
numbers: Human sample 81 people with 18+ responses in both AUTs: jump count test-retest r=0.42 (p<.001, CI [0.22,0.58]). LLM test-retest r=0.22 (CI [0.12,0.31]). Human unique uses: 2,770 (brick), 3,512 (paperclip). Models: several open models plus GPT-4 turbo, Palm bison, Gemini 1.0 pro, Claude 3. On the animal fluency task LLMs were overwhelmingly persistent (p<.001).
limits: Observational across models; one embedding model for categories; Ocsai originality. No intervention that forces switching.
agent_relevance: Gap 7 stays open: nothing here changes the order of seeds. Observation only: flexible search goes with higher originality across LLMs, so test a forced-switch prompt.

source: Schapiro et al. (2026, v6) Measuring combinatorial creativity in LLMs and humans (KOMBINE)
finding: 35 LLMs and 75 humans on association, analogy and blending. Association originality is the best predictor of every other facet. Humans score below nearly every LLM. Models re-use each other's invented properties.
numbers: Association-analogy r=0.71, analogy-blending r=0.70, blending-association r=0.54. Association originality vs analogy originality r=0.73, vs analogy surprise r=0.63, vs blend originality r=0.42, vs blend surprise r=0.50, vs valid blends r=0.48. One in five invented concepts reuses another model's property; same-provider models 2.3 times more likely.
limits: Cross-model correlations (n=35 models), automatic scoring with a three-judge panel. Not a seed-distance manipulation.
agent_relevance: Remote association is a measurable model-level skill that tracks other creative skills; a cheap association probe could pick which model handles open mode.

source: Luchini, Kenett, Zeitlen, Christensen, Ellis, Brewer and Beaty (2023) Convergent thinking and insight problem solving relate to semantic memory network structure
finding: Larger sample (477) from semantic fluency data: high convergent-thinking people had a more interconnected, flexible network; insight solvers had shorter paths than analytic solvers, even with accuracy controlled.
numbers: N=477. Group sizes and effect sizes not available on the abstract page.
limits: Abstract page only. Outcome is convergent thinking (CRA) and problem-solving style, not creativity ratings; fluency-based network, not free association.
agent_relevance: Nearest larger-sample extension of the 2014 direction (shorter paths with better creative-type performance); a conceptual, not exact, replication. Gap 3 still lacks a preregistered replication.

source: Benedek, Kenett, Umdasch, Anderson, Fink and Neubauer (2017) How semantic memory structure and intelligence contribute to creative thought (Thinking and Reasoning)
finding: Per a search summary: creative ability was linked to shorter average path length and higher clustering only under one filtering method (relatedness threshold), not with fixed edge counts or weighted networks. Higher crystallised intelligence went with more flexible structure.
numbers: Not read this session.
limits: Snippet-level; method dependence matches Robinson 2024.
agent_relevance: Same direction as 2014 but method dependent; do not treat as a robust replication.

source: Bernard, Kenett et al. (2019) Building individual semantic networks and exploring their relationships with creativity (CogSci)
finding: Per a search summary: authors report a close relation between creative abilities and individual semantic network metrics, described as replicating and extending earlier findings.
numbers: Not read.
limits: Proceedings paper, snippet only, authors' own framing.
agent_relevance: Same research group, so not independent; still no independent lab or preregistered replication found.

source: Are LLMs becoming similarly creative? Evidence from three years of models (2026)
finding: Re-read for gap 8: 68 models from March 2023 to July 2026 in 12 families, prompts run at temperature and top-p 1.0 with no scaffold; no mitigation tested. Cross-family response distance falls over time.
numbers: AUT (10 prompts) cross-family cosine distance falls from about 0.50 in the earliest bin to below 0.40 in the latest. Second prompt set Infinity-Chat100 (100 prompts) shows the same direction.
limits: No scaffold, persona or seed condition was tested. No claim about a specific model we will use.
agent_relevance: Gap 8 stays open: the homogeneity trend is real across models but no one has tested whether a scaffold reverses it for a given model.
